_comment: Per-framework registry: the reproduction command that re-derives the committed evidence pack, plus the audience brief rendered onto each framework README. CI (_tooling/verify_evidence.py) runs the commands and diffs the result against the committed pack; _tooling/build_evidence_index.py and _tooling/build_briefs.py generate frameworks/EVIDENCE.md and the standalone briefs from this same file.

brief.audience: Negative-news and adverse-media reviewers, and the analysts handling their escalations.
brief.question: Is this negative-news hit actually about our customer, and is what it alleges materially adverse?
brief.never: It never clears a hit on a bare name match with no identifier, and it never decides the relationship. It sorts the queue and writes the basis.

beneficial-ownership-resolution.positive_class: labelled true beneficial owners (aggregate effective ownership at or above threshold, or a control prong)

brief.audience: KYC / CDD onboarding teams, beneficial-ownership analysts, and independent validators.
brief.question: Who ultimately owns or controls this entity, and can any candidate be cleared as below-threshold defensibly?
brief.never: It never files, freezes, rejects, or off-boards. It never auto-clears a candidate while any part of the ownership graph is unresolved, and control without equity is surfaced, never cleared.

brief.audience: KYC / CDD / onboarding teams and the periodic-review function.
brief.question: What risk rating does this customer get, and can I defend how it was reached?
brief.never: It never onboards, exits, or off-boards a customer. A customer carrying a hard risk factor can never be rated LOW, whatever the composite score says.
brief.structural_claim: The claim here is structural, not a hit rate: **no customer carrying a hard risk factor was rated LOW**, and worsening any single factor never lowers the score (the model is monotonic). Both are tested on every run, and the run fails if either breaks.

brief.audience: Data-governance teams, and the screening and monitoring functions that consume their feeds.
brief.question: Is this customer extract fit to screen against, or will it silently miss people?
brief.never: It never drops, imputes, or repairs a record. A feed whose screening-critical fields breach their ceiling can never pass — it routes to a data owner with the full defect list.

entity-resolution-confidence.positive_class: labelled true same-entity pairs (including transliteration, name-order, and partial-identifier variants)

brief.audience: Sanctions and PEP hit adjudicators, KYC identity-resolution and customer-dedup teams.
brief.question: Are these two identity records the same person, different people, or genuinely indeterminate on the evidence?
brief.never: It never clears a hit because two names are spelled differently, and it never merges two records on a name alone — auto-SAME requires a shared strong identifier. Indeterminate routes to review, not to a clear.

brief.audience: Fraud-strategy, fraud-operations, independent-validation, and control teams.
brief.question: Which transaction or session can be approved on a named trusted-continuity cause, and which requires stronger authentication or human review?
brief.never: It never executes a decline, block, freeze, filing, or customer action. Hard recommendations require a named fired fraud rule and corroborating causes; a score alone never decides.
brief.structural_claim: The symmetric claim has two gates: zero confirmed-fraud events may receive APPROVE, and zero legitimate events may receive a hard disposition. Each zero count must also place its exact one-sided 95% upper failure-rate bound at or below 0.1%.

brief.audience: Second-line quality assurance and investigations leads, before a case file closes.
brief.question: Is this finished investigation file structurally sound enough to close?
brief.never: It never re-investigates or overturns a judgement on the merits. It grades the file's structure, and a file with a critical defect can never pass QA no matter how high it scores.

brief.audience: Financial-crime risk teams setting geographic risk ratings, and the correspondent-banking, EDD, and enterprise-risk-assessment functions that consume them.
brief.question: How much inherent financial-crime risk does this jurisdiction carry, and can I show how the score was reached?
brief.never: It never decides whether to enter, exit, bank, or de-risk a market, and it is not a political judgement about a country. It composites public indices into a documented, floored rating and hands the reasoning to a human.
brief.structural_claim: The claim here is structural, not a hit rate: **no jurisdiction carrying a hard-risk designation was ever rated below its mandated floor** — a comprehensive sanctions program or a FATF black listing forces CRITICAL, and a FATF grey listing, an EU high-risk designation, or an INCSR primary-concern listing forces at least HIGH — the score discriminates cleanly across the designed-risk strata, and raising any dimension never lowers the score (the model is monotonic). All three are tested on every run, and the run fails if any breaks.

brief.audience: The new-product approval committee and the financial-crime advisors who brief it.
brief.question: Before we launch this product, how attractive is it to a launderer, and what must be in place first?
brief.never: It never approves anything. It scores, routes, and names the mandatory pre-launch conditions; the committee decides whether to launch.
brief.structural_claim: The claim here is structural: **no proposal carrying a serious hard attribute was tiered LOW**, a prohibited activity is always referred rather than scored around, and worsening any factor never lowers the score. The run fails if any of the three breaks.

brief.audience: Crypto and blockchain-analytics teams screening wallet activity.
brief.question: How exposed is this blockchain address to illicit funds, and how close is that exposure?
brief.never: It never freezes funds, blocks an address, or reports. It distinguishes 'one hop from a mixer' from 'six hops away through an exchange' and hands the analyst the reasoning.

brief.audience: Crypto investigators and anyone who must hand blockchain evidence to a reviewer or a court.
brief.question: Where exactly did each fact in this evidence pack come from, when was it pulled, and can anyone re-check it?
brief.never: It never says who owns an address or whether anything is wrong. It records observations with provenance; attribution is a human act.
brief.structural_claim: The claim here is evidentiary, not statistical: **every captured fact carries its source, retrieval time, and a hash of the exact bytes**; the totals reconcile to the captures with nothing dropped or double-counted; and the same captures re-render byte-for-byte identically months later.

brief.question: Is this customer actually the listed official, and does that listing still carry material risk?
brief.never: It never auto-clears a currently-serving official, a senior former one, or any corroborated identity match — regardless of score.

brief.audience: Independent testing, QA, and internal audit — anyone who samples a control and must defend the conclusion.
brief.question: How many items must I test, which ones, and what do the exceptions I found actually prove?
brief.never: It never grades the control. It hands the tester the exact statistical statement; the tester owns the conclusion.
brief.structural_claim: The claim here is exactness, not accuracy: the sample size and the upper deviation limit are **computed from exact binomial and hypergeometric tail probabilities**, not read off a lookup table, and each is cross-checked against an independent brute-force computation on every run.

brief.audience: Sanctions & screening teams — the analysts who work the alert queue, and the second line reviewing their dispositions.
brief.question: Of the tens of thousands of screening alerts we get a month, which can be cleared with a reason an examiner would accept, and which must a human read?
brief.never: It never auto-blocks a payment, freezes an account, or files anything. It clears an alert only when it can name a provable cause; a bare common-name match with no identifiers always goes to a person.

brief.audience: Transaction-monitoring rule owners and the model-validation function that must challenge them.
brief.question: Is this rule's threshold in the right place, and how do you know?
brief.never: It never changes a live rule. It recommends a threshold with the evidence behind it, and it will never recommend one that pushes detection of suspicious activity below the required floor.
brief.structural_claim: The claim here is a floor, not an accuracy figure: **every recommended threshold still detects at least 95% of the suspicious activity**, and the run fails if any recommendation would push a rule below that line. Rules that currently leak suspicious activity below the line are recommended *down*, never up.

brief.audience: Transaction-monitoring analysts and the investigations team receiving their escalations.
brief.question: Which monitoring alerts are worth an analyst's time, and which can be closed with a documented reason?
brief.never: It never auto-closes a recognised laundering pattern and never files a SAR. Every escalate/close decision is a human one.

brief.audience: Sanctions-list data owners and the screening operations team that depends on their feed.
brief.question: Is our watchlist current, deduplicated across sources, and did anything change since yesterday?
brief.never: It never merges two distinct designated parties — a false merge would erase a designation, and that is a hard build gate. It designates nobody; issuing authorities do.
brief.structural_claim: The claim here is structural: **zero false merges**. Combining two genuinely different designated parties would erase a designation, so the run fails outright if it ever happens — it is a build gate, not a score.
